head.title: Comparing the Xlib and XCB APIs

body.p: This document intends to provide concrete code snippets on how to write code for X11 using the Xlib and XCB libraries. It presents side by side how the same behavior can be coded using the Xlib and XCB libraries.

The first example is based on Christophe Tronche's tutorial (see links below), and then collected from various resources online (such as the website Stack Overflow). The declarations for the library functions are lifted from their manual pages.

The X Window System was developed in the 1980s. It is based on a networked protocol called the X11 protocol, meaning that the program (called the client) and the display (called the server) might be on different machines connected through a network. This also means that all information between the client and the server must be serialized and sent through a socket, even if the two participants are running on the same machine.

On the lowest level, a client must open a connection, negotiate authentication, and then send all instructions to the server as a sequence of bytes. Similarly, all interaction from the server will be received as sequences of bytes, which the client must poll for on the sockets and then parse it.

To make programming more convenient, the Xlib programming library was created that abstracts away most of this functionality. Xlib itself was still considered relatively low level, and it was intended that proprietary higher level widget toolkits based on the Xt Toolkit Intrinsics, such as Motif, X Athena Widgets or OPEN LOOK Intrinsics Toolkit (OLIT) would be used for most programs. This document does not touch on these APIs.

XCB is an alternative programming library developed in the 2000s that offers a much more direct translation to the X11 protocol functionality. It is very similar to Xlib but leaner and with less convenience functionality available. Programming using the two is very similar, which is why this guide was created.

weave.h1: Get a window onto the screen as fast as possible
weave.p: Before anything, we need to include the proper header files.

code.version: #include <X11/Xlib.h>
#include <xcb/xcb.h>

weave.p: First, a connection must be established to the X Window server, the software that displays the windows are retrieves user interactions.
For XCB, get the first screen (a better way would be to get the default screen).
Create a window. For Xlib, this can be done using XCreateSimpleWindow.

code.version:
/* Window XCreateSimpleWindow( Display * display, Window parent, int x, int y, unsigned int width, unsigned int height, unsigned int border_width, unsigned long border, unsigned long background); */
Window window = XCreateSimpleWindow( display, DefaultRootWindow(display), WINDOW_LEFT, WINDOW_TOP, WINDOW_WIDTH, WINDOW_HEIGHT, /* border_width = */ 0, /* border = */ BlackPixel(display, DefaultScreen(display)), /* background = */ WhitePixel(display, DefaultScreen(display)));

weave.p: Or using the more versatile XCreateWindow. Note that Xlib creates the window ID (return with the type Window), whereas for XCB the xcb_generate_id function must allocate it first. This function can be used for all ID allocation.
Make the window appear on screen.
Until now, these commands have been buffered and not sent to the server. A flush instruction is required for them to take effect.
For linking, the library has to be specified.

code.version: gcc -lX11
gcc -lxcb

weave.p: Establish a connection and get the default screen.
Create a window with background and border color set.
We will wait for the MapNotify event so that the window is displayed on screen. Xlib offers the XSelectInput function for this functionality.

code.version: XSelectInput(display, window, StructureNotifyMask);

weave.p: For XCB we need to call xcb_change_window_attributes for this. Note that this could have been passed during window creation, as we will see in a later example.
Make the window appear on screen.
For XCB, the connection must be flushed. Xlib does not require it here, since waiting for events will flush all commands.

Begin the event loop. Wait each iteration until an event is available and then process it. Note that for XCB, the function xcb_wait_for_event allocates a structure on the heap that must be freed with free once it is no longer used.
Check the returned event type.
Set up a graphics context for drawing.
Select the drawing color. For Xlib, we can use the function XSetForeground directly.
However, for XCB we need to use the more general xcb_change_gc function. Note that this could have been set up during creating the graphical context.
Draw a line. Xlib contains a function to draw a single line.

code.version:
/* int XDrawLine( Display * display, Drawable d, GC gc, int x1, int y1, int x2, int y2); */
XDrawLine(display, window, gc, X1, Y1, X2, Y2);

weave.p: Alternatively, Xlib and XCB both have a function to draw a polygonal line.
XCB requires the connection to be flushed. This will happen for Xlib when checking for events. We also need to free the memory allocated for the event variable.
We will need more include files for these examples.

code.version: #include <X11/Xlib.h> #include <X11/Xutil.h>
#include <xcb/xcb.h>

weave.p: After creating the connection and selecting the default screen, create the window and select which events to listen to.
Set the window title. The full title and the iconified title can be different, so both of them need to be set.

code.version:
xcb_change_property( connection, XCB_PROP_MODE_REPLACE, window, XCB_ATOM_WM_NAME, XCB_ATOM_STRING, 8, sizeof WINDOW_TITLE - 1, WINDOW_TITLE);
xcb_change_property( connection, XCB_PROP_MODE_REPLACE, window, XCB_ATOM_WM_ICON_NAME, XCB_ATOM_STRING, 8, sizeof WINDOW_TITLE - 1, WINDOW_TITLE);

weave.p: Closing a window is not an event generated by the X Window Server but rather by the window manager. Therefore it has to be registered on the window first. This is done by retrieving an atom identifier through its name. For XCB this requires starting with WM_PROTOCOLS. In XCB, the request and processing the response is done via two separate functions: xcb_intern_atom and xcb_intern_atom_reply.
Then we intern the WM_DELETE_WINDOW.

code.version: Atom WM_DELETE_WINDOW = XInternAtom(display, "WM_DELETE_WINDOW", false);

weave.p: Finally we change the WM_PROTOCOLS of the window.

code.version: xcb_atom_t atoms[1]; atoms[0] = WM_DELETE_WINDOW; xcb_change_property( connection, XCB_PROP_MODE_REPLACE, window, WM_PROTOCOLS, XCB_ATOM_ATOM, 32, 1, atoms);

weave.p: After mapping the window, we enter the main loop.
Check for window closing, via ClientMessage and checking if the data is WM_DELETE_WINDOW.
On exposure, display a line (instead of MapNotify).
To check keyboard presses and releases:

code.version: case XCB_KEY_PRESS: case XCB_KEY_RELEASE: fprintf(stderr, "Key%s{keycode = 0x%02X, state = 0x%04X}\n", (event->response_type & ~0x80) == XCB_KEY_PRESS ? "Press" : "Release", ((xcb_key_press_event_t *)event)->detail, ((xcb_key_press_event_t *)event)->state );

Track window movements and resizing.
Finally, update the end of loop to quit if the close window button has been pressed.

Using XNextEvent and xcb_wait_for_event will block the running client until an event is available, typically as a result of user interaction. To use the idle time for other things, such as background calculation or animation, it must be checked whether any events are available first.
On exposure, we set a flag to mark needing a redraw.
Register the size of the window on resizing (and before redrawing, wait for a following exposure event).
At the end of the loop we redraw the image.
